rv.q: As Broadway obsesses over youth and revolt, here’s a sweet and wise Broadway play about just wanting your mom and dad to keep on going, to wish they could live forever and to realize that any artist can complain and roar but some wise ones choose instead to render their loved ones immortal.

Though honorable, thoughtful and wonderful to look at, with crafty performances by Danny Burstein, Zoë Wanamaker and especially Nathan Lane, it caulks so many of the book’s expressive cracks that the best thing about it — its mystery — is sealed out.

But if Irving and Jean Sultan come tempestuously into view in Sharr White’s intermittently satisfying play — which had its official Broadway opening Thursday at Studio 54 — the motivations of their adult son Larry (Danny Burstein) remain oddly blurry.

While the intimate and honest views of a family’s inner workings can’t help but touch our hearts at steadily paced moments, Pictures From Home is too blunt in its characterizations, with father and son especially, repeating their arguments and complaints with unstoppable frequency.
The effect is somewhere between stately and stasis.
But both the conflicts at the heart of the play and its social commentary about the 1980s are too mild to yield much actual drama.

For while the production is impeccable and the performances polished and funny, the play, adapted by Sharr White from Larry Sultan ’s memoir-cum-photography book, feels like a snapshot that hasn’t been fully developed, to borrow the handiest simile.

What’s been schlepped to Broadway, however, is the opposite of a striking still whose subjects entice you with their mystery, conceal a secret behind the eyes and leave you wanting to know more about them.
Unfortunately, the precise elements that saturate Sultan’s seminal work wash out Broadway’s “Pictures from Home.”
Sultan’s complexity has been downgraded, by audience-courting ingratiation, to sugared family-comedy formula.
Nice acting and sensitive direction characterize “Pictures From Home,”...But, dramatically speaking, it’s a bore.
Frustratingly, whatever complexity Sultan's memoir holds translates into oversimplified family squabbles in White's script, and is flattened into diluted comedy by Sher.
Playwright Sharr White (The Other Place) finds similar narrative inspiration for this rich drama about the marvels and mysteries of an ordinary family.
Makes you want to seek out an exhibition of Larry Sultan's photographs and study the real Jean and Irv as if you really do know them, even if it is all a matter of theatrical illusion.
That they are played by three terrific theater veterans

“It’s like this extraordinary myth, unfolding in front of you,” Larry says to his father, Irv. “I would even say that it’s the most convincing representation of the myth of the West and the Garden that I’ve ever seen.” “The myth of the West and the Garden?” an incredulous Irv responds.

Nathan Lane, Danny Burstein, and Zoë Wanamaker star in Sharr White’s new Broadway play. It's the cycle of American success: A poor man works hard and becomes rich enough to send his son to art school, where he picks up all sorts of highfaluting notions about truth and narrative that he uses to bite the hand that feeds.
With ample support from its stars and their director, “Pictures From Home” makes that synergy palpable and satisfying.
Not really a play for the ages, Pictures from Home is, nevertheless, such an delightful display of star techniques and temperaments that it can't help but give pleasure.
Photographs and stage play combine to deliver a powerful and sensitive story of family and self-image that most of us will relate to.

Throughout the 1980s, the photographer Larry Sultan spent close to a decade photographing his parents at their kitschy home for what would eventually become Pictures From Home, a photo book that evokes the feeling of the American Dream set out to dry in the Southern California sun.

It's only in the last ten minutes that the show seems to tap into Sultan's work on a deeper level, rather than merely manifest it for the stage, an effort that can often otherwise feel like dancing about architecture.
However much a hallmark achievement the book was as a work of photography, the stage adaptation feels less hallmark than at best harmless.
Not too long after Pictures From Home gets underway, it turns boring and then abusive to the patrons.
Despite their considerable acting chops, the actors fail to convince.

For a play about a man who sacrifices years of just being a son in order to be his parents’ photo-biographer, Pictures from Home seems curiously disinterested in exploring this family, and the conversations they might have, outside of Larry’s photography.
Downright dishonest is White and Lane’s portrayal of Irving Sultan.
Unfortunately these two fine actors fail to establish the essential love-hate connection between their characters.
But the set-up feels so long and labored this stark denouement is blunted by the far-too-meandering thesis that precedes it.
I congratulate those people who could look past the tepid writing and direction.

With its direct audience addresses, clear dramatic structure (scenes are titled on the backdrop), and unforgettable photos taken by Sultan of his family, White’s play is a fine achievement in the theater—augmented by memorable acting and directing.
So, this is a mixed bag, but recommended because it’s an original play starring three Tony types, and it doesn’t cover obvious territory.
So that makes it even more disappointing for me to have to tell you that White and his director Bartlett Sher haven't been as creative in transferring the book's complexities to the stage.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this adaptation of Larry Sultan's photo memoir, with stellar performances from Lane, Burstein, and Wanamaker praised across the board but the play itself faulted for being verbose, unfocused, and overly sentimental.

sg.ra: SeatPlan names Center Orchestra rows E-G as the best seats overall, citing 'a winning mix of perfect proximity and elevated view over the heads in front' on a good rake with a low stage. Headout notes the 'outstanding inclination' keeps sightlines clear from middle rows. AVFMS Row D seat 2: 'Perfect view with unlimited legroom.' 16-row section seats ~350 of the 413 total; low stage means front rows don't require neck strain.

SeatPlan explicitly names Left and Right Mezzanine as 'the best value seats at the Laura Pels Theatre,' citing cheap tickets vs. central Orchestra with 'a clear and close view.' Only 3 rows (AA/BB/CC), under 100 seats — feels intimate and close to stage. Headout confirms 'very little restriction from the Mezzanine overhang at the back' of the Orchestra, meaning the Mezzanine itself is close/low. Row BB flagged by Headout as a specific value row.
